analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC police anticompetitive behavior by tax-exempt nonprofit hospitals.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with 13 days left in the congressional session, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and died without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, the Federal Trade Commission can block anticompetitive mergers and practices by for-profit hospitals, but tax-exempt nonprofit hospital systems are exempt from that enforcement. This two-page bill would close that loophole, letting the FTC treat nonprofit hospitals the same as for-profit ones when they use their market power. It was introduced in the final days of the 117th Congress and never got a committee hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and communities facing consolidated hospital markets. Hospital mergers and dominant-system behavior in a local area tend to raise what patients and insurers pay; giving the FTC authority over tax-exempt hospital systems would give the main federal antitrust cop a tool to challenge those practices when the actor is a nonprofit.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Federal Trade Commission Act so that tax-exempt hospital organizations and cooperative hospital service organizations are covered by the law against unfair methods of competition.

It targets organizations described in section 501(c)(3) of the tax code that are exempt from taxation — the nonprofit hospital systems that today fall outside the FTC's competition enforcement for this purpose.

The practical effect is that the FTC could investigate and challenge anticompetitive conduct or mergers by nonprofit hospital systems, closing a gap in enforcement over a large share of the hospital industry.

analysis.who_pays: Tax-exempt hospital systems, which would lose their exemption from FTC competition enforcement and face the possibility of investigations, merger challenges, and liability for anticompetitive practices. Any resulting constraints on consolidation could also mean less deal-making revenue for hospital advisers and the systems themselves.

drawbacks.text: Nonprofit hospitals are exempt from most federal income tax, and many argue that status reflects a public mission rather than market power; applying antitrust enforcement to them raises questions about whether the FTC would target entities that serve low-income communities, and the bill contains no tailoring to distinguish mission-driven systems from consolidation-driven ones.

The bill adds one sentence of coverage to the FTC Act with no new funding, staffing guidance, or merger-review standards, so its real-world effect would depend heavily on how the FTC chose to use the authority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest in scope: it fixes a specific enforcement gap that has let some of the largest hospital operators escape FTC competition scrutiny, and hospital consolidation is one of the better-documented drivers of higher prices for patients and employers. The cost falls on nonprofit hospital systems that would face litigation and merger risk, and the bill's blunt one-line design offers no safeguards for community hospitals that merge to survive. On balance it is a targeted consumer-protection fix, not a sweeping healthcare overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in the last two weeks of the session and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on December 13, 2022, joined by Representative Victoria Spartz, a Republican.
The same day it was introduced, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
The action history shows no further activity — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill.
The bill had one cosponsor, Representative Spartz, giving it bipartisan sponsorship but very little visible support in its two-week life.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tax-exempt hospital systems are better off, because they keep their exemption from FTC competition enforcement. Members of Congress who preferred no action lost nothing, since a bill introduced with days left in a session carried no political cost to bury.

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to subject tax-exempt hospital organizations to FTC competition enforcement.

for.name: Rep. Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — in the 21 days before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat as sponsor and one Republican cosponsor — but the bill was introduced in the session's final days and no chamber or committee ever voted, so no party-level positions were ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill removes their exemption from FTC unfair-methods-of-competition enforcement, exposing large tax-exempt systems to merger challenges and antitrust liability. Their exemption has allowed dominant local systems to escape scrutiny while consolidation tends to raise prices for patients and insurers.

Insurers negotiate against hospital systems, so stronger antitrust enforcement against dominant hospitals could lower what insurers pay and pass some of that to premiums. But the effect is indirect and depends on competition actually translating into lower prices.
